key_works: Zhang et al. (2021), *A system of coordinated autonomous robots for Lagrangian studies of microbes in the oceanic deep chlorophyll maximum*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.abb9138.

title: Deep-sea soft robots with long-lived useful payloads
open: Combine pressure-tolerant soft locomotion with sustained sensing, communication, and task payloads while maintaining reliable operation over repeated dives.
status: Mariana Trench operation establishes pressure-tolerant locomotion feasibility; payload integration and service life remain separate requirements.
why: Turns an extreme-environment demonstration into a practical scientific platform.
key_works: Li et al. (2021), *Self-powered soft robot in the Mariana Trench*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-020-03153-z.

title: Autonomous underwater repair and connector mating
open: Inspect, clean, align, mate, and verify underwater connectors or repair interfaces despite currents, biofouling, low visibility, and uncertain contact forces.
status: Ocean One demonstrates underwater dexterous interaction; complete autonomous servicing adds diagnosis and verification.
why: Reduces dependence on divers and expensive intervention vessels.
key_works: Khatib et al. (2016), *Ocean One*, DOI:10.1109/MRA.2016.2613281.

title: Autonomous approach to an initially unknown small body
open: Approach, characterize, select a landing site, and land on an unfamiliar asteroid or comet without a ground team resolving each major uncertainty.
status: Integrated autonomous estimation has been studied in realistic blind simulations; end-to-end operational autonomy is a stronger target.
why: Makes exploration scalable to many small bodies.
key_works: Nesnas et al. (2021), *Autonomous Exploration of Small Bodies Toward Greater Autonomy for Deep Space Missions*, DOI:10.3389/frobt.2021.650885.

title: Reliable anchoring and mobility in microgravity
open: Move and manipulate on small bodies with uncertain cohesion and gravity without unintentionally escaping, overturning, or destabilizing the surface.
status: Small-body exploration exposes poorly constrained surface mechanics; terrestrial contact assumptions do not transfer directly.
why: Enables repeated sampling and instrument placement.
key_works: Nesnas et al. (2021), *Autonomous Exploration of Small Bodies*, DOI:10.3389/frobt.2021.650885.

title: Predictive regolith interaction models
open: Predict sinkage, traction, excavation forces, and ejecta across unfamiliar regolith while quantifying uncertainty from sparse measurements.
status: Unexpected surface interactions motivate autonomy and improved physical characterization; a transferable predictive model remains a key target.
why: Prevents immobilization and supports resource extraction.
key_works: Nesnas et al. (2021), *Autonomous Exploration of Small Bodies*, DOI:10.3389/frobt.2021.650885.

title: Autonomous exploration of planetary crevasses and caves
open: Enter, map, sample, and recover from unknown confined terrain while managing contact, communications, energy, and inaccessible failure states.
status: EELS demonstrates integrated autonomy for ice-world exploration scenarios; complete extraterrestrial mission qualification remains a broader target.
why: Opens access to protected geology and potentially habitable environments.
key_works: Vaquero et al. (2024), *EELS*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.adh8332.

title: Onboard scientific novelty assessment
open: Select scientifically valuable observations and samples while distinguishing genuine novelty from sensor artifacts or model failure.
status: Space autonomy includes planning and scientific operations; robust autonomous scientific judgment remains more demanding than navigation.
why: Increases scientific return when bandwidth and communication delays restrict human oversight.
key_works: Nesnas, Fesq, and Volpe (2021), *Autonomy for Space Robots: Past, Present, and Future*, DOI:10.1007/s43154-021-00057-2.

title: Autonomous spacecraft inspection and repair
open: Diagnose an unfamiliar external fault, plan physical access, perform a bounded repair, and verify success under orbital dynamics and delayed human supervision.
status: Space robotics supports inspection and servicing concepts; integrated diagnosis-to-repair autonomy remains a larger capability.
why: Extends spacecraft life and reduces replacement missions.
key_works: Nesnas et al. (2021), *Autonomy for Space Robots: Past, Present, and Future*, DOI:10.1007/s43154-021-00057-2.

title: Capture of uncooperative objects with unknown inertia
open: Safely capture tumbling objects when inertia, flexible appendages, contact properties, and residual motion are uncertain.
status: Space manipulation research addresses rendezvous and contact; unknown target dynamics make safe capture a coupled estimation–control problem.
why: Supports debris removal and servicing of failed spacecraft.
key_works: Nesnas et al. (2021), *Autonomy for Space Robots: Past, Present, and Future*, DOI:10.1007/s43154-021-00057-2.

title: Shared qualification pathways for high-risk space autonomy
open: Establish reusable physical tests, datasets, and flight opportunities that let new autonomy methods accumulate credible evidence without each project financing a complete mission.
status: EELS illustrates the scale of integrated field validation; the proposed gap is reusable qualification infrastructure, not a claim that existing programs are absent.
why: Reduces the barrier between laboratory autonomy and mission eligibility.
key_works: Vaquero et al. (2024), *EELS*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.adh8332.

title: Navigation through simultaneous dust, smoke, and darkness
open: Preserve localization and obstacle detection when several sensing modalities degrade together, including during robot-induced dust clouds.
status: NeBula and CERBERUS demonstrate difficult subterranean autonomy; correlated sensing failures remain a harder operational regime.
why: Supports emergency access where ordinary visual navigation fails.
key_works: Agha et al. (2021), *NeBula: Quest for Robotic Autonomy in Challenging Environments*, arXiv:2103.11470; Tranzatto et al. (2022), *CERBERUS*, arXiv:2201.07067.

title: Communication infrastructure that deploys itself
open: Jointly explore and place relays so that teams preserve useful communication without sacrificing too much exploration capacity or assuming a known radio map.
status: Subterranean systems explicitly manage communications; optimal deployment under uncertain propagation and changing topology remains difficult.
why: Extends autonomy into tunnels and collapsed structures.
key_works: Agha et al. (2021), *NeBula*, arXiv:2103.11470.

title: Traversability assessment for collapse-prone terrain
open: Infer whether rubble, floors, ladders, or coverings can support a robot without using an unsafe full-load test.
status: Legged subterranean exploration demonstrates mobility through difficult terrain; hidden structural integrity requires additional sensing and mechanics.
why: Prevents loss of robots and secondary collapse.
key_works: Tranzatto et al. (2022), *CERBERUS*, arXiv:2201.07067.

title: Victim search with calibrated missed-detection risk
open: Plan search coverage using realistic human detectability through occlusion, heat sources, sound interference, and changing sensor performance.
status: Subterranean exploration and object search provide relevant foundations; human rescue needs calibrated false-negative risk rather than map coverage alone.
why: Makes “searched” a defensible operational claim.
key_works: Agha et al. (2021), *NeBula*, arXiv:2103.11470.

title: Manipulating rubble without destabilizing the scene
open: Remove or reposition debris while predicting support changes and avoiding secondary collapse, trapped-person injury, or blocked escape routes.
status: Field mobility is more mature than autonomous structural intervention; contact-rich scene modification adds consequential hidden mechanics.
why: Moves disaster robots from reconnaissance toward assistance.
key_works: Tranzatto et al. (2022), *CERBERUS*, arXiv:2201.07067; Garrett et al. (2021), *Integrated Task and Motion Planning*, arXiv:2010.01083.

title: Tether and cable management in unknown spaces
open: Navigate while preventing tether snagging, excessive tension, abrasion, and topological entrapment, including reliable retracing and recovery.
status: Confined-space robotic access demonstrates the value of specialized bodies; tether state adds a deformable object that must be controlled continuously.
why: Makes powered and communication-tethered systems operationally reliable.
key_works: Hawkes et al. (2017), *A soft robot that navigates its environment through growth*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.aan3028.

title: Hazard mapping without entering intolerable exposure
open: Locate hazardous gas sources and concentration boundaries while accounting for sensor delay and robot-induced plume disturbance, keeping the platform within its operating limits.
status: Mobile gas localization addresses source finding; simultaneous exposure-constrained exploration adds a safety requirement.
why: Supports safer industrial and emergency reconnaissance.
key_works: Francis et al. (2022), *Gas source localization and mapping with mobile robots: A review*, DOI:10.1002/rob.22109.

title: Rapid deployment by nonexpert response teams
open: Demonstrate that unfamiliar trained responders can transport, initialize, supervise, and recover a robot under time pressure without research-team assistance.
status: Challenging field systems demonstrate integrated capability; deployment burden and operator dependence require separate acceptance testing.
why: Determines whether robots are useful during real incidents.
key_works: Tranzatto et al. (2022), *CERBERUS*, arXiv:2201.07067.

title: Hidden-peduncle localization and cutting
open: Identify and reach the correct fruit attachment point despite occlusion, plant motion, and adjacent stems, without damaging the crop.
status: Harvesting robots demonstrate crop-specific success; system-level reviews continue to identify occlusion and perception-to-action errors.
why: Improves harvest completion and reduces crop damage.
key_works: Bac et al. (2014), *Harvesting Robots for High-value Crops: State-of-the-art Review and Challenges Ahead*, DOI:10.1002/rob.21525.

title: Predicting delayed bruising from robotic handling
open: Estimate later quality loss from contact history, ripeness, temperature, and cultivar, rather than evaluating only visible immediate damage.
status: A 2026 system-level harvesting review emphasizes quality and full-process evaluation; delayed damage requires longitudinal measurement.
why: Prevents apparent harvesting success from destroying saleable value.
key_works: Wang et al. (2026), *System-Level Smart Robotic Harvesting for High-Value Greenhouse Crops: A Review*, DOI:10.3390/agronomy16181795.

title: Ripeness estimation that transfers across cultivars
open: Infer harvest readiness and internal quality across cultivars, seasons, lighting, and growing conditions, with calibrated uncertainty.
status: Agricultural robotics uses multiple sensing approaches; transferable biological-state estimation remains more difficult than appearance classification.
why: Supports selective harvesting at the right time.
key_works: Duckett et al. (2018), *Agricultural Robotics: The Future of Robotic Agriculture*, arXiv:1806.06762.

title: Selective weeding among touching or overlapping plants
open: Remove weeds while preserving crops when their leaves and roots overlap, morphology is unfamiliar, and localization errors could cause irreversible damage.
status: Agricultural robots address weed control; robust discrimination and precise intervention in dense mixed growth remain difficult.
why: Reduces herbicide use without sacrificing crop yield.
key_works: Duckett et al. (2018), *Agricultural Robotics*, arXiv:1806.06762.

title: Robotic pollination with measured ecological consequences
open: Deliver effective pollination while measuring flower damage, reproductive outcomes, pathogen transfer, and effects on natural pollinators.
status: Agricultural automation creates intervention opportunities; successful contact with flowers is not sufficient evidence of agronomic or ecological benefit.
why: Separates a mechanical demonstration from a useful agricultural intervention.
key_works: Duckett et al. (2018), *Agricultural Robotics*, arXiv:1806.06762.

title: Robotic phenotyping without selection bias
open: Estimate crop traits without systematically missing plants that are occluded, damaged, unusually shaped, or difficult for the robot to access.
status: Field robotics enables repeated measurement; accessibility-dependent sampling can bias the inferred biological population.
why: Makes robotic measurements useful for breeding and agronomic decisions.
key_works: Bac et al. (2014), *Harvesting Robots for High-value Crops*, DOI:10.1002/rob.21525.

title: Mobility that minimizes soil compaction
open: Plan agricultural movement using uncertain soil moisture, bearing strength, and crop-root sensitivity while satisfying work and energy requirements.
status: Agricultural robotics motivates lighter and more precise machinery; measuring and optimizing cumulative soil effects is a separate target.
why: Avoids trading labor savings for long-term soil damage.
key_works: Duckett et al. (2018), *Agricultural Robotics*, arXiv:1806.06762.

title: Hygienic food manipulation with reliable recovery
open: Handle variable food items while maintaining cleanability and contamination controls, including recovery from drops, damaged packaging, and fouled grippers.
status: Harvesting and food manipulation show task-specific capability; full-process quality, verification, and recovery remain system-level challenges.
why: Enables practical food automation rather than isolated handling demonstrations.
key_works: Wang et al. (2026), *System-Level Smart Robotic Harvesting for High-Value Greenhouse Crops: A Review*, DOI:10.3390/agronomy16181795.

title: Assembly from unfamiliar parts and instructions
open: Assemble a previously unseen product from its parts and instructions without manually authored motion scripts or precisely staged initial conditions.
status: FurnitureBench provides reproducible long-horizon assembly tasks; unrestricted new-product transfer is a stronger target.
why: Supports high-mix, low-volume manufacturing.
key_works: Heo et al. (2023), *FurnitureBench: Reproducible Real-World Benchmark for Long-Horizon Complex Manipulation*, arXiv:2305.12821.

title: Tight-tolerance insertion under uncertain geometry
open: Complete insertions with small clearances despite part variation, imperfect calibration, compliance, and uncertain friction, without damaging repeated search motions.
status: Learned fine-grained manipulation demonstrates useful insertion-like skills; robust tolerance handling requires explicit contact reasoning.
why: Expands robotic assembly beyond precision fixtures.
key_works: Zhao et al. (2023), *Learning Fine-Grained Bimanual Manipulation with Low-Cost Hardware*, arXiv:2304.13705.

title: Complete wiring-harness installation
open: Route, fasten, connect, inspect, and correct wiring harnesses with flexible branches and visually similar connectors in confined assemblies.
status: Individual deformable-manipulation operations are studied; complete installation combines topology, force control, and electrical verification.
why: Targets a persistent labor-intensive manufacturing operation.
key_works: Zhu et al. (2022), *Challenges and Outlook in Robotic Manipulation of Deformable Objects*, arXiv:2105.01767.

title: Damage-aware disassembly for reuse
open: Disassemble unfamiliar used products despite hidden fasteners, corrosion, adhesive bonds, and prior damage while preserving valuable components.
status: Assembly benchmarks provide reusable manipulation foundations; used-product disassembly adds uncertain history and destructive alternatives.
why: Enables remanufacturing and higher-value recycling.
key_works: Heo et al. (2023), *FurnitureBench*, arXiv:2305.12821.

title: Closed-loop construction with variable local materials
open: Fabricate structures using materials whose properties vary during production, while verifying geometry and structural performance as construction proceeds.
status: The Digital Construction Platform demonstrated architectural-scale on-site fabrication; adaptive structural qualification remains a broader target.
why: Supports construction outside tightly controlled factories.
key_works: Keating et al. (2017), *Toward site-specific and self-sufficient robotic fabrication on architectural scales*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.aam8986.

title: Construction sequences that remain stable at every step
open: Plan assembly and temporary support so that partially built structures remain stable despite placement error, wind, and uncertain material properties.
status: Termite-inspired construction demonstrates decentralized building; general structural stability throughout assembly is a stronger requirement.
why: Prevents collapse during automated construction.
key_works: Werfel, Petersen, and Nagpal (2014), *Designing Collective Behavior in a Termite-Inspired Robot Construction Team*, DOI:10.1126/science.1245842.

title: Logistics fleets that recover from physical exceptions
open: Restore useful flow after shifted pallets, damaged packaging, fallen goods, blocked aisles, or failed docking—not merely replan around a static obstacle.
status: Multi-agent pathfinding addresses coordinated movement; operational exceptions often require manipulation and workflow repair.
why: Reduces the human exception-handling burden in automated facilities.
key_works: Stern et al. (2019), *Multi-Agent Pathfinding*, arXiv:1906.08291; Garrett et al. (2021), *Integrated Task and Motion Planning*.

title: Human–robot production that improves actual worker outcomes
open: Optimize throughput together with fatigue, musculoskeletal load, workload variability, and worker control, measured over real shifts rather than brief laboratory trials.
status: A 2024 review found substantial gaps between laboratory HRI studies and industrial mobile-robot use.
why: Prevents efficiency gains from concealing displaced ergonomic burdens.
key_works: Haney and Liang (2024), *A literature review on safety perception and trust during human-robot interaction with autonomous mobile robots that apply to industrial environments*, DOI:10.1080/24725838.2023.2283537.

title: Tissue-damage-aware autonomous manipulation
open: Control tissue interaction using patient-specific estimates of tearing, ischemia, crushing, and deformation limits rather than generic force thresholds.
status: Surgical autonomy demonstrates selected tasks; safe tissue interaction remains dependent on anatomy and material variation.
why: Makes autonomy medically meaningful rather than merely geometrically accurate.
key_works: Attanasio et al. (2021), *Autonomy in Surgical Robotics*, DOI:10.1146/annurev-control-062420-090543.

title: Generalization across unfamiliar anatomy
open: Execute a defined surgical procedure across clinically relevant anatomical variation, disease states, and visual conditions, with calibrated limits and escalation.
status: SRT-H demonstrates long-horizon surgical steps and generalization in experimental settings; broad clinical coverage is a stronger target.
why: Avoids dependence on narrowly selected anatomical examples.
key_works: Kim et al. (2025), *SRT-H: A Hierarchical Framework for Autonomous Surgery via Language Conditioned Imitation Learning*, arXiv:2505.10251; DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.adt5254.

title: Autonomous verification of surgical completion
open: Verify that a surgical step achieved its intended physiological result and did not create hidden damage, rather than inferring success from instrument motion.
status: Autonomous anastomosis and learned surgical tasks provide important demonstrations; functional verification remains a separate requirement.
why: Detects incomplete closure, leaks, retained material, or incorrect tissue handling.
key_works: Saeidi et al. (2022), *Autonomous robotic laparoscopic surgery for intestinal anastomosis*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.abj2908; Kim et al. (2024), *Surgical Robot Transformer*, arXiv:2407.12998.

title: Needle steering with uncertain tissue motion
open: Reach targets while avoiding critical structures when tissue deforms, moves physiologically, and differs from preoperative models.
status: Autonomous medical needle steering has been demonstrated in vivo; robust transfer across anatomical and motion conditions remains a broader target.
why: Improves minimally invasive access to difficult targets.
key_works: Kuntz et al. (2023), *Autonomous medical needle steering in vivo*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.adf7614; Alterovitz et al., *A Review of AI Guidance for Medical Motion Planning*, DOI:10.1146/annurev-control-032024-024305.

title: Predicting collateral thermal damage
open: Estimate and control subsurface thermal injury during robotic energy-based treatment despite uncertain tissue properties, perfusion, and sensor visibility.
status: Surgical autonomy integrates sensing and control, but visible tool placement alone cannot certify thermal effects.
why: Protects structures outside the immediate treatment target.
key_works: Attanasio et al. (2021), *Autonomy in Surgical Robotics*, DOI:10.1146/annurev-control-062420-090543.

title: Recovery from unexpected bleeding or tissue failure
open: Detect a deviation, stabilize the situation, preserve clinician control, and execute a validated fallback when a planned surgical step fails.
status: SRT-H advances multistep autonomy; emergency recovery requires a separately demonstrated safety capability.
why: Addresses the failures that matter most clinically.
key_works: Kim et al. (2025), *SRT-H*, arXiv:2505.10251.

title: Surgical training data with realistic rare complications
open: Build ethically collected, well-annotated datasets covering rare complications, interventions, anatomical variation, and failed attempts—not only successful nominal procedures.
status: SRT demonstrates learning from surgical demonstrations; rare-event coverage and intervention provenance are additional dataset requirements.
why: Enables evaluation of failure handling without relying on unsafe trial-and-error.
key_works: Kim et al. (2024), *Surgical Robot Transformer: Imitation Learning for Surgical Tasks*, arXiv:2407.12998.

title: Clinical evidence for increasing surgical autonomy
open: Establish trial designs and outcome measures that attribute benefits and harms to the autonomous component, including escalation, operator workload, and post-market changes.
status: A 2024 study classified autonomy in FDA-cleared robots over its historical study period; laboratory capability and clinical authorization are distinct evidence questions.
why: Supports responsible transition from experimental autonomy to clinical practice.
key_works: Lee et al. (2024), *Levels of autonomy in FDA-cleared surgical robots*, DOI:10.1038/s41746-024-01102-y.

title: Safe feeding across variable food and user states
open: Acquire, transport, and present diverse foods while adapting to user motion and readiness, with explicit handling of spills, failed bites, and swallowing-related limits.
status: Haptic food-manipulation research addresses acquisition; complete safe assistance requires user-state and delivery reasoning.
why: Supports greater independence during meals.
key_works: Bhattacharjee et al. (2019), *Towards Robotic Feeding: Role of Haptics in Fork-Based Food Manipulation*, IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters 4(2):1485–1492.

title: Dressing across garments and mobility limitations
open: Dress users with different body shapes, pain constraints, involuntary motion, and limited mobility using unfamiliar garments while preventing harmful contact.
status: Deep haptic model-predictive control demonstrated gown dressing with human participants; broad garment and user coverage remains open.
why: Addresses a high-value daily assistance task.
key_works: Erickson et al. (2018), *Deep Haptic Model Predictive Control for Robot-Assisted Dressing*, arXiv:1709.09735; DOI:10.1109/ICRA.2018.8460656.

title: Patient transfer with uncertain body support
open: Assist transfers between beds, chairs, and standing while inferring load distribution, user participation, pain, and balance without unsafe probing.
status: Safe physical HRI provides relevant methods; transfer assistance requires whole-body support and individualized constraints.
why: Reduces injury risk for users and caregivers.
key_works: Lasota, Fong, and Shah (2017), *A Survey of Methods for Safe Human-Robot Interaction*, DOI:10.1561/2300000052.

title: Exoskeleton assistance across real-world transitions
open: Adapt assistance through stairs, slopes, turning, speed changes, stopping, and irregular surfaces without destabilizing the wearer.
status: Real-world personalization has been demonstrated; reliable transitions across diverse daily activities remain a broader target.
why: Extends benefits beyond steady treadmill walking.
key_works: Slade et al. (2022), *Personalizing exoskeleton assistance while walking in the real world*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-022-05191-1.

title: Personalization for changing impairment and fatigue
open: Optimize assistance as a user’s strength, fatigue, pain, and recovery evolve, without burdensome repeated laboratory calibration.
status: Human-in-the-loop optimization demonstrated individualized walking assistance; clinical and time-varying personalization introduces additional constraints.
why: Makes assistance responsive to the person rather than a fixed average model.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2017), *Human-in-the-loop optimization of exoskeleton assistance during walking*, DOI:10.1126/science.aal5054.

title: Stable neural control over months and years
open: Maintain prosthetic or robotic control despite changes in neural signals, electrode interfaces, user strategies, and physiological state.
status: Brain–computer interfaces demonstrate meaningful robotic control and sensory feedback; long-term stability remains a distinct translational target.
why: Reduces recalibration burden and unreliable access to assistive functions.
key_works: Flesher et al. (2021), *A brain-computer interface that evokes tactile sensations improves robotic arm control*, DOI:10.1126/science.abd0380.

title: Useful artificial touch beyond laboratory tasks
open: Deliver tactile feedback that consistently improves everyday manipulation, embodiment, and safety across users and object classes.
status: Evoked tactile sensations improved robotic arm control in a published BCI study; broad daily-life benefit requires additional evidence.
why: Restores information essential to natural dexterity.
key_works: Flesher et al. (2021), *A brain-computer interface that evokes tactile sensations improves robotic arm control*, DOI:10.1126/science.abd0380.

title: Assistive robots that remain useful after deployment
open: Demonstrate sustained home use accounting for setup, cleaning, repairs, caregiver effort, abandonment, and changing user needs.
status: The WHO–UNICEF assistive-technology report documents broader access and service challenges; robot-specific longitudinal service models require evidence.
why: Ensures that technical capability translates into durable independence.
key_works: WHO and UNICEF (2022), *Global Report on Assistive Technology*, ISBN:9789240049451.

title: Legible motion for diverse observers
open: Generate motions that communicate intent across differences in experience, culture, attention, and physical ability without sacrificing safety or task feasibility.
status: Legibility and predictability were distinguished experimentally in 2013; generalization across users and contexts remains a broader target.
why: Reduces surprise and improves coordination.
key_works: Dragan, Lee, and Srinivasa (2013), *Legibility and predictability of robot motion*, IEEE ICRA.

title: Trust calibrated to actual robot competence
open: Help users rely on robots appropriately as competence changes, rather than maximizing trust or perceived friendliness.
status: A 2024 review identifies measurement and field-validation gaps in safety perception and trust.
why: Prevents both dangerous overreliance and unnecessary rejection.
key_works: Haney and Liang (2024), *A literature review on safety perception and trust during human-robot interaction with autonomous mobile robots that apply to industrial environments*, DOI:10.1080/24725838.2023.2283537.

title: Field-valid measures of perceived and actual safety
open: Establish measures that distinguish feeling safe from being safe and predict behavior during prolonged real-world interaction.
status: The same 2024 review found predominantly controlled laboratory experiments and limited industrial-platform coverage.
why: Prevents questionnaire improvements from being mistaken for reduced harm.
key_works: Haney and Liang (2024), *A literature review on safety perception and trust…*, DOI:10.1080/24725838.2023.2283537.

title: Human interaction with multiple simultaneous robots
open: Design coordination and signaling that remain understandable when several robots move and act around the same people.
status: Human–robot safety methods often focus on individual interactions; combined robot behavior introduces attention and predictability problems.
why: Enables warehouses, hospitals, and public spaces with genuine fleets.
key_works: Lasota et al. (2017), *A Survey of Methods for Safe Human-Robot Interaction*, DOI:10.1561/2300000052.

title: Negotiating autonomy and consent during tasks
open: Let users grant, limit, revise, and revoke task authority in ways the robot can interpret and enforce during ongoing physical work.
status: Language-grounded affordance systems support instruction following; authority negotiation requires more than selecting an executable skill.
why: Preserves meaningful user control.
key_works: Ahn et al. (2022), *Do As I Can, Not As I Say*, arXiv:2204.01691.

title: Transparent teleoperation over variable networks
open: Provide convincing force and motion feedback despite variable delay, packet loss, and model mismatch while preserving stability.
status: Passivity-based methods solved important delay-stability problems; high transparency under realistic network and contact conditions remains a tradeoff.
why: Improves remote intervention without hiding dangerous contact forces.
key_works: Anderson and Spong (1989), *Bilateral control of teleoperators with time delay*, DOI:10.1109/9.24201; Wang (2021), *Bilateral control of teleoperator systems with time-varying delay*, DOI:10.1016/j.automatica.2021.109707.

title: Handover timing under uncertain human readiness
open: Transfer objects when the human is ready and supporting the load, while handling distraction, hesitation, weakness, or unexpected withdrawal.
status: Safe physical HRI provides relevant sensing and control methods; readiness is a hidden human state rather than a fixed trajectory event.
why: Makes routine collaboration comfortable and safe.
key_works: Lasota et al. (2017), *A Survey of Methods for Safe Human-Robot Interaction*, DOI:10.1561/2300000052.

title: Long-term psychosocial effects of social robots
open: Determine which forms of repeated social-robot interaction produce durable benefits or harms, separating novelty effects, selection bias, and displacement of human contact.
status: Social interaction and ethics were identified among robotics’ grand challenges; longitudinal causal evidence remains the appropriate target.
why: Prevents adoption based solely on short-term engagement.
key_works: Yang et al. (2018), *The grand challenges of Science Robotics*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.aar7650.

title: Open-world road-scene understanding
open: Detect and reason about unusual road configurations, temporary instructions, debris, emergency activity, and objects outside the training taxonomy.
status: Autonomous-driving systems have mature perception pipelines; uncommon combinations and open-set conditions remain fundamental challenges.
why: Addresses failures not represented by ordinary object-detection benchmarks.
key_works: Yurtsever et al. (2020), *A Survey of Autonomous Driving: Common Practices and Emerging Technologies*, arXiv:1906.05113.

title: Joint uncertainty over interacting road users
open: Predict multiple agents’ futures with calibrated joint distributions that preserve dependence and respond correctly to the ego vehicle’s actions.
status: Large motion-forecasting datasets support interaction modeling; accurate joint counterfactual prediction is stronger than marginal trajectory prediction.
why: Prevents planners from combining individually plausible but mutually inconsistent futures.
key_works: Ettinger et al. (2021), *Large Scale Interactive Motion Forecasting for Autonomous Driving: The Waymo Open Motion Dataset*, arXiv:2104.10133.

title: Negotiation without aggressive or exploitable behavior
open: Merge, cross, and yield effectively when other drivers adapt to the robot, without becoming either dangerously assertive or indefinitely passive.
status: Interactive driving is widely studied; guarantees under uncertain human response remain challenging.
why: Makes autonomous vehicles socially functional in mixed traffic.
key_works: Yurtsever et al. (2020), *A Survey of Autonomous Driving*, arXiv:1906.05113.

title: Risk-aware handling of occluded road users
open: Choose speed and position using uncertainty about unseen pedestrians or vehicles without assuming that every occlusion contains an adversarial actor.
status: Multimodal driving datasets improve visible-scene understanding; occluded-agent risk requires additional models and validation.
why: Balances safety with usable progress.
key_works: Caesar et al. (2020), *nuScenes: A multimodal dataset for autonomous driving*, arXiv:1903.11027.

title: Statistically credible rare-event safety validation
open: Demonstrate acceptable serious-failure rates without relying on infeasibly large undifferentiated road-mile totals or unvalidated simulation extrapolation.
status: Kalra and Paddock quantified limitations of mileage-based reliability demonstrations; combining evidence sources remains an important problem.
why: Makes safety claims testable at realistic cost.
key_works: Kalra and Paddock (2016), *Driving to safety: How many miles of driving would it take to demonstrate autonomous vehicle reliability?*, DOI:10.1016/j.tra.2016.09.010.

title: Sensor-fusion robustness under adverse weather
open: Preserve calibrated perception when rain, snow, fog, glare, dirt, and spray simultaneously affect several sensors in correlated ways.
status: Multimodal datasets provide important baselines; sensor diversity does not eliminate common environmental failure modes.
why: Expands dependable operating conditions.
key_works: Caesar et al. (2020), *nuScenes*, arXiv:1903.11027.

title: Safe fallback when stopping is itself hazardous
open: Select a minimum-risk response to failure when an immediate stop could cause a collision or leave the vehicle in an unsafe location.
status: Autonomous-driving architectures include fallback behavior; appropriate risk minimization depends on traffic, road geometry, and remaining capabilities.
why: Makes system failure handling context-sensitive.
key_works: Yurtsever et al. (2020), *A Survey of Autonomous Driving*, arXiv:1906.05113.

title: Cooperative driving with untrusted or missing infrastructure data
open: Use vehicle and infrastructure messages without becoming unsafe when messages are delayed, incorrect, unavailable, or inconsistent with onboard observations.
status: Interactive motion modeling and connected operation offer benefits; dependence on external information creates additional uncertainty and security constraints.
why: Enables cooperation without making connectivity a safety prerequisite.
key_works: Ettinger et al. (2021), *Large Scale Interactive Motion Forecasting for Autonomous Driving*, arXiv:2104.10133.

title: Benchmarks that measure intervention-free completion
subfield: Datasets, benchmarks, software, and computing infrastructure
open: Evaluate complete workflows while counting every reset, teleoperation episode, scene adjustment, and human recovery action.
status: FurnitureBench offers reproducible long-horizon physical tasks; an intervention-complete accounting standard is an additional requirement.
why: Makes benchmark scores comparable to actual autonomous usefulness.
key_works: Heo et al. (2023), *FurnitureBench*, arXiv:2305.12821.

title: Robot-data provenance with physically meaningful metadata
subfield: Datasets, benchmarks, software, and computing infrastructure
open: Record calibration, embodiment, control mode, operator intervention, sensor timing, licensing, and environmental conditions in machine-checkable dataset provenance.
status: Datasheets establish a general documentation framework; robotic data require additional physical and temporal semantics.
why: Supports trustworthy reuse and diagnosis of transfer failures.
key_works: Gebru et al. (2021), *Datasheets for Datasets*, arXiv:1803.09010; Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al. (2023), *Open X-Embodiment*, arXiv:2310.08864.

title: Simulator rankings that predict physical rankings
subfield: Datasets, benchmarks, software, and computing infrastructure
open: Establish when a simulator benchmark correctly ranks competing methods on real robots, including uncertainty over rank reversals.
status: Simulation suites such as SoftGym support controlled comparisons; predictive validity for physical deployment requires paired experiments.
why: Prevents optimization of benchmarks that select the wrong methods.
key_works: Lin et al. (2020), *SoftGym*, arXiv:2011.07215.

title: Shared corpora of failures and recoveries
subfield: Datasets, benchmarks, software, and computing infrastructure
open: Collect representative failed attempts, near misses, interventions, and successful recoveries with sufficient context to study failure mechanisms.
status: DROID expands real-world manipulation data; a failure-centered corpus has different sampling and annotation requirements.
why: Enables research on reliability rather than only imitation of successful behavior.
key_works: Khazatsky et al. (2024), *DROID*, arXiv:2403.12945.

title: Public contact and wear reference datasets
subfield: Datasets, benchmarks, software, and computing infrastructure
open: Publish synchronized force, geometry, material, environmental, and degradation measurements that support cross-simulator and cross-sensor validation.
status: Contact-model comparisons establish the importance of modeling choices; broad physical reference data would make those comparisons more decisive.
why: Anchors simulation and tactile learning to measured mechanics.
key_works: Le Lidec et al. (2024), *Contact Models in Robotics: a Comparative Analysis*, arXiv:2304.06372.

title: End-to-end real-time guarantees for modern robot stacks
subfield: Datasets, benchmarks, software, and computing infrastructure
open: Bound sensing-to-actuation latency when neural inference, middleware, logging, networking, and multiple controllers share heterogeneous processors.
status: ROS 2 addresses production-oriented middleware requirements; application-wide worst-case timing requires additional analysis.
why: Makes control assumptions valid under actual system load.
key_works: Macenski et al. (2022), *Robot Operating System 2: Design, Architecture, and Uses In The Wild*, arXiv:2211.07752.

title: Portable skill interfaces with executable contracts
subfield: Datasets, benchmarks, software, and computing infrastructure
open: Define skills that expose preconditions, effects, uncertainty, resource needs, authority requirements, and recovery behavior across robot platforms.
status: Generalist datasets and policies share experience; portable execution semantics require more than common action tensors.
why: Reduces repeated integration while preserving correctness.
key_works: Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al. (2023), *Open X-Embodiment*, arXiv:2310.08864; Garrett et al. (2020), *PDDLStream*, arXiv:1802.08705.

title: Accessible shared physical evaluation facilities
subfield: Datasets, benchmarks, software, and computing infrastructure
open: Establish remotely accessible, independently operated robot test facilities with maintained hardware, standardized resets, and transparent queueing and costs.
status: Open datasets lower one access barrier; independent physical replication still requires equipment and operational support.
why: Allows more researchers to test claims without building duplicate laboratories.
key_works: Chi et al. (2024), *Universal Manipulation Interface*, arXiv:2402.10329; Khazatsky et al. (2024), *DROID*, arXiv:2403.12945.

title: Cybersecurity metrics that reflect physical consequences
subfield: Security, governance, funding, and public goods
open: Quantify robotic vulnerabilities using potential physical harm, recoverability, exposure, and compensating controls—not only conventional software severity.
status: Robotics cybersecurity research advocates robot-specific risk assessment; calibrated physical consequence models remain necessary.
why: Helps prioritize defenses that protect people and equipment.
key_works: Dutta and Zielińska (2021), *Cybersecurity of Robotic Systems: Leading Challenges and Robotic System Design Methodology*, DOI:10.3390/electronics10222850.

title: Enforceable authority boundaries for language-controlled robots
subfield: Security, governance, funding, and public goods
open: Ensure that text, images, external documents, and third-party messages cannot authorize physical actions beyond the user’s current permissions.
status: Language-generated robot programs expand interfaces; secure delegation must distinguish task content from authenticated authority.
why: Prevents untrusted observations from becoming commands.
key_works: Liang et al. (2022), *Code as Policies*, arXiv:2209.07753; Dutta and Zielińska (2021), *Cybersecurity of Robotic Systems*, DOI:10.3390/electronics10222850.

title: Security updates that preserve physical safety
subfield: Security, governance, funding, and public goods
open: Deploy patches to long-lived robots while preserving timing, calibration, control behavior, and rollback capability, including during interrupted updates.
status: Robot cybersecurity and production middleware address parts of the problem; security and safety assurance must be composed.
why: Avoids choosing between vulnerable software and unvalidated behavior changes.
key_works: Dutta and Zielińska (2021), *Cybersecurity of Robotic Systems*, DOI:10.3390/electronics10222850; Macenski et al. (2022), *Robot Operating System 2*, arXiv:2211.07752.

title: Privacy-preserving robot incident reporting
subfield: Security, governance, funding, and public goods
open: Create interoperable reporting of injuries, near misses, interventions, and failures while protecting people, confidential environments, and legitimate proprietary information.
status: NIOSH’s robotics program studies occupational risks; the proposed target extends surveillance into reusable, privacy-preserving incident data.
why: Allows the field to learn from failures that individual organizations may rarely observe.
key_works: NIOSH (2024), *Center for Occupational Robotics Research*; Gebru et al. (2021), *Datasheets for Datasets*, arXiv:1803.09010.

title: Durable funding for independent long-term replication
subfield: Security, governance, funding, and public goods
open: Establish financing and publication incentives for independent multi-month replication, maintenance reporting, and negative results.
status: Risk-management frameworks emphasize measurement and monitoring; sustained independent robotic replication is the proposed public-good target, not a quantified claim of zero existing funding.
why: Tests whether reported capabilities survive different teams and operating conditions.
key_works: NIST (2023), *Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)*, DOI:10.6028/NIST.AI.100-1.

title: Repairability and end-of-life support for deployed robots
subfield: Security, governance, funding, and public goods
open: Develop sustainable technical and commercial arrangements for spare parts, calibration data, security maintenance, and safe retirement after vendors or product lines disappear.
status: Robotics’ grand challenges include materials, power, and societal integration; this target concerns lifetime support rather than initial capability.
why: Prevents expensive robots from becoming unusable or unsafe stranded assets.
key_works: Yang et al. (2018), *The grand challenges of Science Robotics*, DOI:10.1126/scirobotics.aar7650.

title: Evidence and payment models for useful assistive robots
subfield: Security, governance, funding, and public goods
open: Establish procurement or reimbursement models that reward measured independence, caregiver burden reduction, reliability, and ongoing service rather than device purchase alone.
status: WHO and UNICEF document assistive-technology access and service challenges; robot-specific outcome and payment evidence remains necessary.
why: Connects effective technology to users who cannot finance experimental products.
key_works: WHO and UNICEF (2022), *Global Report on Assistive Technology*, ISBN:9789240049451.

title: Worker participation in robotic deployment decisions
subfield: Security, governance, funding, and public goods
open: Develop and evaluate deployment processes that let affected workers influence task allocation, monitoring, safety controls, training, and recourse.
status: Occupational robotics research addresses emerging workplace risks; the unresolved target is a validated participatory deployment model.
why: Improves the chance that automation delivers shared benefits rather than merely shifting risk.
key_works: NIOSH (2024), *Center for Occupational Robotics Research*; NIST (2023), *AI Risk Management Framework 1.0*.
